rows.definition: Free of what obstructs, and easy to understand. Also to remove — the same word for the state and the act of reaching it.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: Free of what obstructs, and easy to understand — also, as a verb, the act of reaching that state by removing what was in the way.
rows.historical_meaning: Old French cler, from Latin clarus (bright, clear, famous); the 'to remove' sense is a later verbal extension of the state of being unobstructed.

rows.definition: A surface where a system is spoken to in typed commands. The oldest interface, and still the most exact.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: A surface where a system is spoken to in typed commands — the oldest interface this house keeps, and still among the most exact.
rows.historical_meaning: Initials of 'command line interface': command from Latin commandare (com- together + mandare, to entrust), line from Latin linea (a linen thread, a marked line), interface from Latin inter- (between) + facies (face, form); the oldest way of speaking to a machine, one line at a time.

rows.definition: A single deliberate press. Also the sound of one — the interaction named for the noise it made.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: The interaction borrowed its name from a byproduct — the sound was never the point of the press, only evidence that the press had happened, and the word kept that evidence's name long after the mechanisms that made the actual noise disappeared.
rows.historical_meaning: Middle English clicken, likely imitative of the sound itself and reinforced by Dutch klikken; the word sounds like the thing it names, in the same pattern as 'bubble.'

rows.definition: That which asks, in a system where something else answers. Also one served under an obligation of care.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: Both senses put the asking party in the weaker position — a client depends on an answer it cannot compel, whether the one owing that answer is a server across a network or a professional bound by duty, and the obligation runs in one direction only.
rows.historical_meaning: Latin cliens/clientem (a follower, a dependent), from clinare (to lean, to bend); a client was, at the root, one who leaned on a patron for protection and favour.

rows.definition: The instrument that tells the hour honestly — in this house, a reading is always taken, never assumed.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: The instrument that tells the hour honestly — in this house, a reading is always taken fresh, never assumed from memory.
rows.historical_meaning: Middle Dutch clocke (bell), from Medieval Latin clocca (bell), possibly of Celtic origin; the earliest mechanical timepieces were named for the bell they struck, not for the face they later grew.

rows.definition: To bring to an end, and to shut. Also nearness — the same word for ending a thing and for being beside it.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: To bring to an end, and to shut — also nearness itself, one word serving both an ending and a proximity.
rows.historical_meaning: Old French clos, from Latin claudere (to close, to shut); the nearness sense grows from the idea of a gap being shut down to almost nothing.

rows.definition: Command shortened to its shell name — the word an instruction answers to.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: Command shortened to its shell name — the word an instruction actually answers to when it is typed rather than spoken.
rows.historical_meaning: Clipped from command, Old French comander, from Latin commandare (com- together + mandare, to entrust, to order).

rows.definition: A cut fragment as it appears in this library, not an English word. Flagged for the mis-cut band rather than defined.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: A fragment left over from an imperfect cut through this library's source text, not a word in its own right — kept exactly as found, so the mis-cut stays visible rather than being smoothed away.

rows.definition: Together with. A part placed at the front to make an act shared.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: Together with — a part set at the front of a word to make the act that follows a shared one rather than a solitary one.
rows.historical_meaning: Latin com- (a variant co- appears before vowels and h), from cum (with, together); a prefix that makes whatever it attaches to a shared act.

rows.definition: Instructions written so a machine can carry them out. Also any system where one thing stands for another by agreement.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: The two senses share a hinge on trust rather than on mechanism — a machine does exactly what it is told whether or not the instruction was wise, and a cipher works only for as long as both sides keep faith with the same agreement, so code is the word for exactness that depends on nothing verifying it in the moment.
rows.historical_meaning: Old French code, from Latin codex/caudex (the trunk of a tree; a block of wood; and, since wooden tablets were bound for writing, a book of laws); instructions a machine carries out share the name with the oldest bound law-books.

rows.definition: The bound book of standards — and the Council seat of taxonomy, structure, and knowledge. A codex is where scattered pages become one authoritative volume.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: Binding is the whole act — loose pages carry the same words as a codex but not the same authority, because a codex asserts that everything inside its covers belongs together and nothing outside them is part of the standard it keeps.
rows.historical_meaning: Latin codex, an alternate spelling of caudex (the trunk of a tree, a block of wood); Roman writing tablets of wood, and later bound sheets of parchment, kept the name of the material they began as.

rows.definition: Cofra (Irish cófra: a chest, a coffer). A zip archive read and written with no dependency at all, which is to say a box with the list of what is in it fastened inside the lid. Entries are STORED or DEFLATE and nothing else. CRC-32 is computed over every entry AS IT IS READ and checked against the directory, and a mismatch names the entry and both values rather than returning a shorter file and calling it success. Zip64, encryption and every other compression method are REFUSED BY ENTRY NAME — method 12 is named bzip2, 99 is named AES, and a method the table does not know is refused by its number rather than guessed at — because a silent skip is the one failure a container must never have. An entry with no date takes the DOS epoch, 1980-01-01, the earliest an MS-DOS date field holds, which is the whole reason the same content written twice is the same bytes twice: nothing here ever asks the clock. The reader finds the end record by scanning back for its signature and confirming its comment length lands exactly on the end of the file; it reads the central directory rather than trusting the local headers' sizes, because flag bit 3 may defer them; it slices a stored entry rather than viewing it, so one small file cannot hold a whole archive in memory behind it; a trailing slash over zero bytes is a folder marker and is skipped; and a repeated name is refused in both directions rather than resolved. THE PLATFORM PRIMITIVE IS NEVER IMPLEMENTED: the host surface names raw deflate in both directions and nothing else — no level, no strategy, no dictionary, because the moment a host may be tuned two hosts stop writing the same bytes — and two reference hosts on two unrelated machines, the platform's own CompressionStream and node:zlib, are proven byte-for-byte identical rather than promised. No keys, no passwords, no ciphers, and no verb on the surface that could hold one. No disk, no clock, no network, zero runtime dependencies.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: A zip archive read and written with no outside dependency — a box that carries its own list of what is inside it, fastened into the lid.
rows.historical_meaning: Irish cofra (a chest, a coffer), itself likely borrowed from Old French cofre / English coffer, ultimately from Greek kophinos (a basket, a hamper) — the tool's own name is Irish, but that word already carries a longer loan history behind it.

rows.definition: Belonging to knowing and thinking. Of the processes by which a mind takes in and works on what it meets.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: Names the machinery rather than its output — calling a process cognitive says something about how a mind arrived at a result, never whether that result was correct, wise, or even attended to as reasoning while it was happening.
rows.historical_meaning: Latin cognoscere (to get to know, to become acquainted with), from co- (together, thoroughly) + gnoscere (to know), from a root for knowing.

rows.definition: The state of parts holding together without contradiction. Coherence is not truth; it is the absence of self-conflict.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: The state of parts holding together without contradicting one another — coherence is not truth; it is only the absence of a part fighting another part.
rows.historical_meaning: Latin cohaerere (to cling together, to be connected), from co- (together) + haerere (to stick, to cling).

rows.definition: Short form of column. One upright division of a grid or table.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: Short for 'column' — the single letters standing in for the upright division of a table or a grid.
rows.historical_meaning: Clipped from column (Latin columna, a pillar); see column.

rows.definition: A Prism syntax theme of cool darkness — the name enters as itself, a dress code wears.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: Names one particular syntax-highlighting theme of cool darkness — a named style a piece of software wears, not a general concept.
rows.historical_meaning: A modern coinage blending cold (Old English cald) and dark (Old English deorc) into a single theme name; no independent ancient root sits behind the compound, only behind its two halves.

rows.definition: Working together such that the result belongs to more than one. Collaboration keeps each hand visible rather than merging them.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: Working together such that the result belongs to more than one — collaboration keeps every hand visible rather than folding them into one.
rows.historical_meaning: Latin collaborare (to work together), from com- (together) + laborare (to labour, to work), from labor (toil).

rows.definition: Made by more than one hand, with each hand still visible. Of work that belongs to a group without belonging to nobody.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: Visibility is the test that separates this from mere delegation — a thing made collaboratively still shows the seams where one hand's work meets another's, and smoothing those seams away until no hand can be told from any other would turn collaboration into something else entirely.
rows.historical_meaning: From collaborate (Latin collaborare, com- + laborare, to work together); see collaboration.

rows.definition: Those who build a thing together, each with their own hand in it. Collaboration keeps every contributor visible.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: Those who build a thing together, each with their own hand still visible in it once it is done.
rows.historical_meaning: From collaborate (Latin collaborare, com- + laborare, to work together); see collaboration.

rows.definition: Folded down so its contents are out of sight. Present and not shown — the state is closed, not empty.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: Closed and empty look the same from outside and are not the same claim — a collapsed state promises its contents are still there, merely not currently shown, so opening it again should only reveal what was inside rather than rebuild it.
rows.historical_meaning: Latin collabi (to fall together, to give way), from com- (together) + labi (to slide, to fall).

rows.definition: To gather things together on purpose. Collecting is what makes a set out of scattered instances.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: To gather things together on purpose — collecting is exactly what turns scattered instances into a set.
rows.historical_meaning: Latin colligere (to gather together, to bind up), from com- (together) + legere (to gather, to choose, to read).

rows.definition: Things gathered and kept together on purpose. What makes it a collection is the gathering, not the likeness.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: Two collections can hold nothing alike and both be genuine, because the bond a collection asserts is that someone chose to keep these particular things as one set, not that the things share a nature — break the deliberate keeping and the same objects become a mere pile.
rows.historical_meaning: From collect (Latin colligere, com- + legere, to gather); see collect.

rows.definition: Many acting as one without ceasing to be many. A collective is a direction of attention, not a merger - the individuals are still there.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: Many acting as one without ceasing to be many — a collective is a shared direction of attention, not a dissolving of the individuals inside it.
rows.historical_meaning: From collect (Latin colligere, com- + legere, to gather); collective describes a direction shared by many rather than a merger of them into one.

rows.definition: The page where a work's making is recorded — who, how, and with what hands.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: The colophon is the one page in a work that speaks about the work rather than in its voice — it steps outside the telling to say who actually did the telling, which is this house's own habit of leaving a record of hands rather than letting a finished thing pretend it made itself.
rows.historical_meaning: Greek kolophon (a summit, a finishing touch); the page at a book's end that records how it was made borrows the word for the last stroke that completes a thing.

rows.definition: Light's name — the visual channel of the sensory lexicon, where a meaning is seen before it is read. Every atom in this Grammar carries one.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: Light's own name — the visual channel of this Grammar's sensory register, where a meaning is seen before it is ever read. Every atom here carries one.
rows.historical_meaning: Latin color (colour, hue), possibly related to celare (to hide, to cover), from a root for concealment — colour, on this reading, is what covers a surface.

rows.definition: An upright division, in a structure or a table. Both a support that bears load and a field that holds one kind of thing.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: The two senses share a shape rather than merely a word — a column holding up a roof and a column holding one kind of value both work by standing apart from their neighbors and carrying only their own share, so removing one changes what the whole can bear without touching any other column at all.
rows.historical_meaning: Latin columna (a pillar), related to collis (a hill), from a root meaning to rise; a column is, at the root, a thing that stands up.

rows.definition: To bring separate things into one while each remains recognisable. Combination joins; it does not dissolve.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: To bring separate things into one while each stays recognisable — combination joins two things; it does not dissolve either of them.
rows.historical_meaning: Latin combinare, from com- (together) + bini (two at a time), from bis (twice).

rows.definition: Work made to produce laughter, and the shape of a story that ends well. Both are about relief arriving.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: Work made to produce laughter, and also the shape of a story that ends well — both are, at bottom, about relief finally arriving.
rows.historical_meaning: Greek komoidia, from komos (a revel, a merry-making procession) + aeidein (to sing); comedy was first specifically a sung, festive performance before it named a shape of story that ends well.

rows.definition: The absence of strain a body registers before the mind notices. Comfort is a design outcome, not a luxury.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: The absence of strain a body registers before the mind has caught up to notice it — comfort, read this way, is a design outcome rather than a luxury.
rows.historical_meaning: Old French conforter, from Late Latin confortare (to strengthen greatly), from com- (thoroughly) + fortis (strong); comfort meant giving someone strength before it meant giving them ease.

rows.definition: Free of strain a body would register. Comfort is a design outcome, not a luxury.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: Free of the strain a body would otherwise register — comfort treated as something built in, not something indulged.
rows.historical_meaning: From comfort (Late Latin confortare, to strengthen) + -able; see comfort.
